prize_parts.citation: For the conception and leadership of the ATLAS and CMS experiments that led to the discovery of the Higgs boson.

statement.case_for: The experimental discovery of the Higgs boson completed the Standard Model and confirmed electroweak symmetry breaking. The 2013 prize recognised the theoretical proposal, so the measurement itself is unrecognised. Two independent general-purpose detectors, ATLAS and CMS, found a narrow signal in enormous backgrounds, which is the clearest possible case of detector-driven discovery with built-in redundancy. A decade of coupling and mass measurements has matured the result fully. I would credit the people who conceived and led the two projects, since the detectors were the enabling achievement: Jenni and Della Negra as founding spokespersons of ATLAS and CMS, and Virdee as CMS project leader. Four colleagues (Danielsson, Mehlig, Olsson, Eriksson) put B020 in their top eight, and Danielsson ranks it first, so it has support from experimentalists and theorists alike. That is more than the first-place counts suggest.
statement.case_against: Any collaboration prize forces three individuals to stand for thousands of people, and the choice among Jenni, Della Negra, Virdee and Gianotti is inevitably contestable. Leadership of a detector project is different from the analysis leadership at the moment of announcement, and a prize built on the first may be read as ignoring the second. There is also a risk that the Higgs discovery is seen as an extension of the 2013 award rather than a distinct achievement. Finally, B020 is the one candidate where my own instrumentalist bias is most likely to inflate the case, so I should discount my own enthusiasm.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B020 first and proposes Gianotti, Della Negra and Jenni, with Virdee as an equally defensible CMS choice, and notes that balance between the two experiments is a real difficulty.
responses.response: I agree that balance between ATLAS and CMS is the central difficulty, but I differ on the names. Gianotti led ATLAS when the discovery was announced, which is a real argument. However, the prize here is for building the experiments, and on that logic Jenni and Della Negra founded the projects and Virdee ran CMS construction as project leader. Choosing Jenni plus two CMS figures leaves the ATLAS side with one name, which I accept because Jenni's role as founder and long-time spokesperson was central. I would still be open to swapping Virdee for Gianotti if the committee decides the discovery announcement, not the construction, is the achievement being honoured.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B041 first as a clean theory-plus-experiment story, but flags that the supplied credit omits the first-author experimentalist and that the Higgs discovery is outside his own subfield.
responses.response: I take the omission point seriously, and it weakens B041 as a three-name prize: the experimental discovery of correlated states in twisted bilayer graphene involved early-career co-authors who cannot be credited here. I also note that the eight-year-old field still disputes the origin of its superconductivity, whereas the Higgs result is settled and independently confirmed. I do not dismiss B041 and would keep it in play, but I do not think the attribution difficulty is lower there than for B020. Eriksson's ranking B020 eighth also seems to me to reflect subfield distance more than the strength of the case.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B003 first, arguing that light-matter interfaces are the enabling architecture for quantum networks and repeaters, with Kimble, Rempe and Lukin a defensible trio.
responses.response: I accept that the science is serious, but I disagree on timing. Kroll's own text concedes that a repeater-based network is not yet demonstrated, and Johansson notes the field is only moderately mature. B003 is also a compound field in which the 2012 prize already honoured Haroche and Wineland, and Cirac, Zoller and Duan supplied decisive proposals that are not in this credit. I would rather wait until the application is realised than award now on promise.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B001 first, as an experimental trio of Bloch, Greiner and Esslinger who made a controllable laboratory for strongly correlated statistical systems, with over twenty years of replication.
responses.response: I agree that B001 is the strongest non-Higgs candidate on maturity and breadth, and that is why it is my first alternative. My reservation is the theory-experiment allocation: Mehlig and I both exclude Zoller and Cirac, but Johansson ranks them first in B011, and Zoller's lattice proposal is arguably the intellectual origin of the Mott experiments. If the committee prefers a prize on this field, I would want the committee to settle that split explicitly rather than by default.

uncertainties: Which three individuals best represent ATLAS and CMS, and in particular whether Gianotti should replace Virdee or Della Negra.
Whether a prize for experiment construction and leadership is preferred over one for the discovery analysis and announcement.
Whether the committee should split the prize across two achievements, which the three-person limit makes difficult when B020 alone already needs three names.
How much weight to give to B001 as a competitor, given the unresolved theory-experiment allocation with B011.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B020: my documented collaborations are PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGOLite/PoGO+ and XL-Calibur, none of which are in any shortlisted entry. My doctoral work at Birmingham and CERN was in experimental particle physics, but the profile does not identify the experiment, and I cannot say whether it involved any credited person. I disclose this and my general instrumentalist preference for detector-driven discovery so that colleagues can weigh my ranking accordingly. As Chair, I would not claim to have special knowledge of ATLAS or CMS roles.
